question.:question/problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}3x{y}^{2}\,dx+4{x}^{2}y\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise, what expression belongs in the blank after applying Green's theorem and changing to polar coordinates $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, with the integrand simplified pointwise before integration?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186176024/plots/circle-3.png)

Since $P(x,y)=3x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=4{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=6xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=8xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}3x{y}^{2}\,dx+4{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8xy-6xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
